chunks: And from him, from Ahmad ibn al-Hasan, from his father, from Ahmad ibn 'Umar ibn Abi Shu'bah, from his father, from Abu 'Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said:
He was asked about the wealth of an orphan, so he said: 'There is no zakat upon it unless it is traded with.'
As for the saying of the Sheikh (Al-Shaykh al-Tusi), may God have mercy on him: whenever it is traded with, zakat becomes obligatory upon it.

He means by it recommendation and preference, rather than obligation and compulsion, because there is no difference between it being traded with or not being traded with regarding the fact that zakat does not become obligatory upon it with the obligation of compulsion, by which leaving it incurs punishment.

Do you not see that if this wealth belonged to a mature adult and he traded with it, zakat would not become obligatory upon it with the obligation of compulsion, as we will clarify later, if God Almighty wills.
And that which indicates that zakat becomes obligatory upon it with this type of obligation when it is traded with is what he narrated:
ai.seo_question: Is zakat obligatory on an orphan's wealth if it is not invested?
ai.summary: In *Tahdhib al-Ahkam*, Shaykh al-Tusi elaborates on the juristic distinction between obligatory (wajib) and recommended (mandub) zakat for orphans' wealth, citing Imam al-Sadiq's ruling that liability arises only upon commercial investment. The scholar clarifies that this 'obligation' is of the recommended type rather than strict compulsion, drawing a parallel to the ruling for mature adults to emphasize that non-payment incurs no punitive consequence, reflecting the nuanced Shia approach to minor's assets.
